title: Password Storage and Authentication
subtitle: bcrypt, Argon2id, salting, work factors, and secure credential handling

whyItExists.problem: Databases get breached. If passwords are stored in plaintext or with fast hashes (SHA-256, MD5), attackers can crack millions of passwords in hours using GPUs. 85% of breached passwords are cracked within 24 hours if hashed with MD5.
whyItExists.solution: Purpose-built slow password hashing algorithms (bcrypt, Argon2, scrypt) make brute-force attacks impractical by being intentionally slow and memory-intensive. Salts prevent precomputed rainbow table attacks.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any system that stores user passwords. Never store passwords in plaintext. Never use fast hashes (MD5, SHA-256, SHA-1) for passwords.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Passwords should ideally not be stored at all — use OAuth/OIDC (sign in with Google/GitHub) to delegate authentication. Store passwords only when necessary.

explainModes.beginner: Password hashing is like a one-way grinder. You put a password in, get a scrambled string out, and you can never reverse it. When users log in, you grind their attempt and compare the results — you never need the original.
explainModes.simple: Unlike SHA-256 (which runs in microseconds), bcrypt takes ~100ms per hash intentionally. An attacker with a GPU can try 10 billion SHA-256 hashes per second, but only ~40 bcrypt hashes per second. Argon2 is even more resistant.
explainModes.standard: Password hashing algorithms: automatically generate a salt (prevents rainbow table attacks), apply many rounds of an expensive function (cost parameter / work factor), and produce a self-contained hash string containing algorithm, salt, cost, and hash. Argon2id is the OWASP 2024 recommendation.
explainModes.technical: Argon2 has three variants: Argon2d (GPU-resistant via memory access), Argon2i (side-channel resistant), Argon2id (hybrid — recommended). Parameters: time_cost (iterations), memory_cost (RAM in KB), parallelism (threads). bcrypt uses 2^cost rounds of Blowfish key setup.
explainModes.deepDive: The PHC (Password Hashing Competition, 2013-2015) evaluated 24 algorithms and selected Argon2. PBKDF2 is FIPS-approved but less resistant than Argon2 — use if FIPS compliance is required. The need_rehash() function (argon2-cffi) detects when stored hashes use outdated parameters and transparently upgrades on login.

content.text: Why Fast Hash Algorithms Are Dangerous for Passwords

Passwords must never be stored in plaintext or with fast hash functions like MD5 or SHA-256. These produce a hash in microseconds. An RTX 4090 GPU can test 184 billion MD5 hashes per second — an 8-character password falls in seconds. Purpose-built password hashing algorithms are intentionally slow.

a.name: SHA-256 (WRONG for passwords)
a.useWhen: Never for passwords. Use for file integrity, signatures, HMAC.

b.name: Argon2id (CORRECT for passwords)
b.description: Password hashing — slow and memory-intensive by design
strengths: Memory-hard: requires GB of RAM (limits GPU parallelism)
b.useWhen: All password storage. Configure work factor so hashing takes 100-500ms on your server.

content.definition: A unique random value added to each password before hashing. Prevents precomputed rainbow table attacks: even if two users have the same password, their hashes are different.
A parameter that controls how slow the hash is. Increasing it by 1 doubles the work. Set it so hashing takes 100-500ms on your hardware. Increase it as hardware gets faster.

content.code:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError, VerificationError

# --- Configure Argon2id (OWASP 2024 recommendations) ---
ph = PasswordHasher(
    time_cost=3,        # iterations (higher = slower)
    memory_cost=65536,  # 64 MB RAM required per hash (limits GPU attacks)
    parallelism=4,      # threads
    hash_len=32,        # output hash length
    salt_len=16,        # salt length (auto-generated)
)

# --- Hash at registration ---
password = "user_password_here"
hash_string = ph.hash(password)
print(hash_string)
# $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$<salt>$<hash>
# The hash string contains: algorithm, params, salt, hash — all in one

# --- Verify at login ---
try:
    ph.verify(hash_string, password)
    print("Password valid")
    # Upgrade outdated hash parameters if needed
    if ph.check_needs_rehash(hash_string):
        new_hash = ph.hash(password)
        # Save new_hash to DB
except VerifyMismatchError:
    print("Wrong password")
except VerificationError as e:
    print("Verification error:", e)

import bcrypt

# --- Hash password (bcrypt handles salt automatically) ---
password = b"user_password"  # must be bytes
cost = 12  # 2^12 = 4096 rounds; adjust until hash takes ~100ms

hash_bytes = bcrypt.hashpw(password, bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=cost))
print(hash_bytes)  # b'$2b$12$<22-char-salt><31-char-hash>'

# --- Verify ---
if bcrypt.checkpw(password, hash_bytes):
    print("Valid")
else:
    print("Invalid")

# --- IMPORTANT: bcrypt truncates at 72 bytes ---
# If password > 72 bytes, all bytes beyond 72 are ignored!
# Mitigation: SHA-256 the password first, then bcrypt
import hashlib, base64

def hash_password_safe(password: str) -> bytes:
    # SHA-256 first to handle long passwords, then bcrypt
    prehash = base64.b64encode(hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).digest())
    return bcrypt.hashpw(prehash, bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12))

content.text: bcrypt silently truncates passwords at 72 bytes. If a user's password is 73+ characters, bcrypt treats it the same as the first 72 bytes. For long password support, pre-hash with SHA-256 before bcrypt, or switch to Argon2id which has no length limit.

content.code:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError
import hmac

ph = PasswordHasher(time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536, parallelism=4)

# --- Registration ---
def register_user(username: str, password: str, db) -> None:
    if len(password) < 12:
        raise ValueError("Password too short")
    hashed = ph.hash(password)
    db.execute("INSERT INTO users (username, password_hash) VALUES (?, ?)",
               (username, hashed))

# --- Login ---
def login_user(username: str, password: str, db) -> bool:
    row = db.execute("SELECT password_hash FROM users WHERE username = ?",
                     (username,)).fetchone()
    if not row:
        # Still hash to prevent timing-based username enumeration
        ph.hash("dummy_to_prevent_timing")
        return False

    try:
        ph.verify(row["password_hash"], password)
        # Transparently upgrade hash if params are outdated
        if ph.check_needs_rehash(row["password_hash"]):
            db.execute("UPDATE users SET password_hash = ? WHERE username = ?",
                       (ph.hash(password), username))
        return True
    except VerifyMismatchError:
        return False

content.text: Always hash a dummy password on failed username lookups to prevent timing-based username enumeration. If the lookup is instant for unknown users (no DB hit) but slow for known users (bcrypt runs), an attacker can enumerate valid usernames by measuring response times.

questions.question: Why are bcrypt/Argon2id preferred over SHA-256 for password storage?
options: They produce longer hashes that are harder to crack
They are intentionally slow and memory-intensive, making brute-force attacks impractical
They are easier to implement correctly
They require a secret key, adding an extra security layer
questions.explanation: Password hashing algorithms are designed to be slow (~100ms) and memory-intensive. This limits GPU-based brute force to ~40 hashes/second instead of 10 billion.

questions.question: What does a 'salt' do in password hashing?
options: It is added to the password before hashing to ensure each hash is unique
It is a secret key stored in the KMS
It compresses the password before hashing
questions.explanation: A salt is a unique random value added to each password before hashing. It ensures two users with the same password get different hash outputs, defeating precomputed rainbow table attacks.

questions.question: What is the OWASP 2024 recommended algorithm for password hashing?
questions.explanation: Argon2id is the OWASP 2024 top recommendation. It is memory-hard (limits GPU parallelism), has no known vulnerabilities, and was the PHC competition winner.

faq.q: Should I add my own salt to Argon2 or bcrypt?
faq.a: No. Argon2 and bcrypt include automatic, cryptographically secure salt generation. The salt is embedded in the hash output string. Adding your own salt on top provides no benefit and may introduce bugs.

faq.q: How do I migrate from MD5/SHA-1 password hashes?
faq.a: On next login: verify the old hash, re-hash the plaintext password with Argon2id, store the new hash, delete the old one. Mark a column to track which hashes have been upgraded. For accounts that never log in again, force password reset on their next login attempt.

An application-wide secret value added to all passwords before hashing (in addition to the per-user salt). The pepper is stored outside the database (e.g., in an env var or KMS). Even if the database is breached, attackers cannot crack passwords without the pepper.

examples: The 2012 LinkedIn breach exposed 6.5 million unsalted SHA-1 hashes; 90% were cracked within days
Django uses PBKDF2-SHA256 by default and transparently upgrades to Argon2 when the argon2-cffi package is installed
bcrypt was designed in 1999 specifically for password hashing and remains secure today because its cost parameter can be increased
